Additionally, we demonstrate that certain access structures, known as Fr\'echet structures, have intricacy comparable to standard access structures, while also showing that certain secret-sharing schemes, known as matrix schemes, have intricacy comparable to random access structures. This research provides a new approach to evaluating the efficiency of access structures, which can aid in the selection and design of these structures for secure computation protocols.

Determining the degree of entanglement between two remote qubits, linked by an lossy environment, poses an significant challenge. Standard measures, such as the von Neumann entropy, often overestimate entanglement due to the influence of decoherence. To overcome this limitation, a different approach based on the geometric measure of entanglement is presented, offering an optimal method for quantifying entanglement in presence of decoherence. This approach has been successfully demonstrated in experiments involving four optical qubits, showing that the geometric measure of entanglement provides a more accurate representation of entanglement degradation due to decoherence and environmental noise.

The latest research findings on palm tree modes (PTM) observed in the JET tokamak are presented. A comprehensive review of the underlying physics and observational characteristics of PTMs, along with an analysis of their features, is provided. Evidence suggests that PTMs are a manifestation of the edge of a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) eigenmode. Statistical correlations indicate a strong connection between PTM frequency and plasma density, with scaling consistent with the $nq_{95}$ relationship. Observations of PTM rotation frequencies and associated driving and damping processes are presented. It is proposed that PTMs are a result of an ideal magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode with characteristics of an Eulerian path MHD mode.

Continual Learning (CL) research focuses on developing AI models that can adapt to new information without compromising previous knowledge. Despite ongoing efforts, deep neural networks often struggle to retain pre-existing knowledge effectively. This study challenges the widespread reliance on advanced pre-trained models by proposing a straightforward yet effective CL approach for classification tasks. Our method, based on standard cross-entropy loss, outperforms existing techniques across multiple CL scenarios and initial model architectures. Furthermore, it is compatible with a broad range of neural network designs, easy to implement, and efficient in terms of computational requirements. Our work aims to stimulate a more critical examination of the extensive use of pre-trained models in CL research.

One of the most pressing challenges in developing trustworthy AI for vulnerable groups lies in creating effective models to identify and classify abusive speech across different languages and platforms. Despite significant progress in this area, the full potential of multi-modal approaches, which incorporate text and visual modalities, has yet to be realized. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative model that integrates text and image modalities, thereby setting a new standard for abuse speech classification and providing deeper insights into abusive content. Our proposed model, which is trained on the Twitter abuse dataset, achieves exceptional performance, outperforming existing state-of-the-art single and multi-modal models. Furthermore, through detailed analysis, we demonstrate that the model's image-based predictions offer valuable interpretability advantages, making it an attractive solution for large-scale, real-time abuse speech classification applications on social media platforms.

This study examines the effects of degree distributions on the dynamics of homogeneous and heterogeneous networks of Type-I neurons. We investigated how different degree distributions influenced the emergence of synchronized neural activity in these networks. Compared to networks designed to model real-world systems, homogeneous networks exhibited more frequent and easier transitions into synchronized states. Homogeneous networks also displayed robust synchronized states, particularly in regards to periodic oscillations. However, the synchronized states shown by homogeneous networks in certain scenarios surpassed those shown by heterogeneous networks across all scenarios. These findings highlight the significant impact of degree distributions on the dynamics of neural networks, emphasizing the importance of accurately modeling the connections within complex systems to accurately predict their behavior.

Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of semantic patch, a code mutation technique, in automatic program repair. However, applying code transformations that mirror human intentions is a complex task, requiring the identification of relevant program elements. This paper introduces a novel approach, adversarial mask generation, to tackle the challenge of generating applicable code transformations by employing a neural network to mask irrelevant program elements. Empirical evidence from four repair benchmarks indicates that adversarially generated masks yield higher repair success rates compared to masks produced through random mask generation. The implementation details can be found at: https://github.com/chenyuan1230/AdvMask.

This paper introduces a novel approach to achieve the capacity region of the Gaussian identity-interference-quantization combined (GIFC) channel through an innovative information spectrum method. The method first establishes a connection between the GIFC channel and a family of generalized GIFC channels with diverse input distributions. It then establishes a relationship between the GIFC channel and a specific binary Gaussian channel, enabling the derivation of a lower bound on the capacity region. By employing a novel information spectrum method, we demonstrate that any achievable rate pair of the GIFC channel must fall within a specific region bounded by two capacities, one of which is the binary Gaussian channel capacity. Ultimately, we utilize this approach to prove that the capacity region of the GIFC channel includes a rectangle with bounds determined by the binary and binary-symmetric AWGN channel capacities.

Using advanced analysis techniques, researchers investigate the behavior of heavy-ion collisions in relativistic experiments. A novel method for studying these interactions involves employing 3-dimensional flow assessments, where initial and final data on particles are correlated to determine specific collision characteristics. Similar to the Rapidity Rapidity ratio, the Flow assessment provides critical information on collision geometry and the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, according to computer simulations. An alternative to traditional flow measurements, the Flow assessment offers enhanced capabilities for studying relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has prompted the development of predictive models to aid in early detection, contact tracing, and risk assessment. In the UK, various initiatives, such as NHS Test and Trace, have been implemented to curb the outbreak. Our research explores the application of adversarial training techniques in COVID-19 risk assessment models to improve their robustness and resilience. By pitting a risk assessment model against an adversary, the model is forced to be more specific and resistant to manipulation. Our approach enhances the model's ability to perform effectively even when provided with adversarially selected risk features. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of this technique, with models that have been adversarially trained displaying improved performance on real-world risk datasets.

In wireless communication systems equipped with multiple antennas, effective channel estimation is vital for optimizing data transmission. Graph neural networks (GNNs), a type of machine learning tool, have shown promise in assisting with this process. This research paper explores two GNN-based methods for channel estimation: a centralized approach that aggregates local information from individual antennas to produce an accurate, comprehensive map; and a decentralized method that enables each antenna to utilize its individual findings, allowing the network to collectively learn a collective channel model. Our study reveals that decentralized networks can still achieve high accuracy, even in scenarios where some antennas lack direct communication with others, and further demonstrates that decentralized networks scale more efficiently to handle an increased number of antennas compared to centralized ones.

The trend of increasing homicide rates in Brazil is notable, with some states experiencing more severe rises in violence than others. Goias, a midwestern state, has seen its homicide rates fluctuate over the years, differing significantly from national and regional trends. This study aims to identify the factors contributing to the spikes in violence in Goias, specifically examining the years 2008 and 2012, when homicide rates surpassed national averages. Using data from the Brazilian Ministry of Health's Information System on Homicide, the research team analyzed the social, economic, and institutional characteristics of municipalities in Goias that experienced significant increases in violence. Cluster analysis revealed correlations between homicide rates and key factors, such as regional divisions, education levels, and economic conditions.

We examine how the variance of stochastic gradient gradients affects the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ in non-accelerated stochastic gradient descent to $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{t})$ in accelerated stochastic gradient descent. We propose a new adaptive algorithm that increases the step size when the gradient variance is high and decreases it when the variance is low, achieving an improved convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$. We also investigate the accelerated variant, where the algorithm adapts to the variance to attain a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{t})$. We validate the success of these algorithms through numerical experiments in quadratic programming.

Axions emerge as a necessary consequence in theories that extend the standard model of particle physics, particularly in theories that involve the proliferation of certain particles. Axions tend to be produced in the Sun due to the natural occurrence of processes that convert them. As a result, existing observations of the Sun can potentially be used to investigate the properties of axions. However, this can only be done effectively if a sufficient number of axions are detected, which requires a significant number of events. This can be achieved through the use of a highly sensitive axion detector, such as BabyIAXO. This document presents a study on how BabyIAXO can be used to investigate various aspects of the Sun's core. This includes the determination of the Sun's core temperature, composition, and characteristics based on data from solar neutrinos. This study demonstrates that BabyIAXO can make meaningful contributions to our understanding of the Sun's core, particularly in the context of astrophysical research.

The existence of non-trivial stationary solutions for the linearized ZK equation is proven, which has implications for the original nonlinear equation, leading to the existence of unique, non-oscillating solutions. Moreover, it has been observed that these solutions can be unstable and cause the original ZK equation to exhibit periodic behavior. The existence of such periodic solutions is attributed to the non-local characteristic of the ZK equation. The possibility of extending these findings to other equations, particularly Airy equations, is also discussed.

Developing robots with dexterous manipulation capabilities that can effectively handle a wide variety of objects is a highly challenging task within the realm of robotics. A crucial aspect of achieving this goal involves creating an extensive dataset that enables robots to perform successful grasps on diverse items. However, existing grasp datasets face significant limitations due to their restricted scope and reliance on actual robotic experiments, which are often time-consuming and expensive to implement. To address these shortcomings, we have designed and constructed DexGraspNet, a comprehensive simulated grasp dataset tailored for dexterous manipulation. By leveraging advances in machine learning and the capabilities of the game engine Unity, our dataset encompasses a vast array of possible grasps on numerous objects, which have been meticulously annotated for further analysis. Additionally, our research showcases the effectiveness of a pre-trained policy network derived from the Soft Actor-Critic framework in accurately predicting grasping actions for various dexterous robots, which is a crucial step towards achieving robust manipulation tasks. By leveraging the vast resources of the DexGraspNet dataset, researchers and engineers can accelerate their development of dexterous robots capable of effectively grasping and manipulating a wide variety of objects.

A novel four-dimensional turbo spin echo sequence has been developed for acquiring high-resolution T2-weighted images of the abdominal cavity without interruption. By employing an advanced technique to mitigate effects from organ movement during imaging, the new sequence provides rapid acquisition times. A study comparing the new approach with existing techniques found that the new approach matches the image quality of conventional methods while a faster scanning time is achieved. A significant reduction in organ movement during imaging is observed with the new approach. A clinical trial was conducted to assess the new approach's performance in imaging the liver, pancreas, and aorta. By utilizing the new approach, the new 4D turbo spin echo sequence was found to provide high-quality images of the abdominal cavity without interruption.

Recent advancements in model compression through knowledge distillation have yielded impressive results, with many current methods focusing on mirroring the teacher model's output. This paper reveals the existence of an alternative, more effective approach to model compression. By preserving information flow rather than output, it is possible to achieve superior performance. The proposed InDistill method addresses this concept by utilizing intermediate knowledge to compress models, with significant improvements demonstrated in various tasks, including image and language processing.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and we examine the topological properties of the level sets of these functions. We show that if the level sets of one function intersect the level sets of another function at a finite number of points, and the ratio of the functions approaches a finite number as it tends to infinity, then the topological structure of the sets defined by these functions is similar. We also find that if the level sets of two functions intersect each other at a finite number of points, and the ratio of the functions approaches a finite number as it tends to infinity, then the foliations of the plane defined by these functions are topologically equivalent when the ratio of the functions is greater than one. This equivalence extends to the study of pseudoholomorphic foliations for functions that satisfy a certain linear-like condition.

Ecosystems that thrive in arid regions are particularly susceptible to changes brought about by human activity and environmental shifts. Two key factors that influence these changes are the management of grazing spaces and the climate's variability due to temperature fluctuations. Research has previously focused on the immediate effects of these factors, but the goal of this study is to investigate how the interaction between grazing and climate conditions impacts the dynamics of arid vegetation. By combining mathematical theories related to phase transitions and the movement of particles with information on grazing practices and climate data from a specific region in Australia, this study demonstrates that vegetation patterns can be significantly affected by both the management of grazing and the climate's variability.

A crucial technique known as CountSketch efficiently generates probabilistic sketches of large datasets, which are then analyzed using smaller representations. This method employs random matrices to track the counts of specific elements in large datasets, and has been extensively used for tasks like linear sketching, sketching submodular functions, and more. However, traditional studies have focused on non-adaptive inputs, whereas our research investigates how CountSketch performs under adaptive inputs. We demonstrate that when faced with adaptive inputs, popular variants of CountSketch fail to provide the guaranteed bounded approximation ratio. Nevertheless, we also develop a new variant that achieves bounded approximation for adaptive inputs while ensuring linear processing time and space. This outcome is particularly significant, as it implies that sketching tasks can be efficiently solved in near-linear time even when dealing with adaptively chosen inputs.

A comprehensive description is provided for ipie, a Python-based program that utilizes auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo for computational chemistry calculations. Key aspects of ipie are discussed including its flexible algorithm structure, adaptability across various platforms, and incorporation of high-performance computing techniques. Furthermore, ipie is evaluated through a series of challenging total-energy and free-energy calculations for molecules and nanostructures, showcasing its performance improvements when utilizing multiple GPUs and mixed CPU-GPU configurations. Additionally, ipie is compared to other popular quantum chemistry programs in a range of applications.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from quantum computing due to its potential to rapidly process complex algorithms and navigate intricate market connections. However, traditional high-frequency trading tactics may be undermined by quantum uncertainty versus entanglement utilization. This study examines the application of quantum principles in high-frequency trading through two primary approaches. Firstly, a quantum prisoner's dilemma game represents a scenario in which two traders must decide whether to collaborate on a trade or pursue individual interests. This decision-making process is complicated by a unique form of quantum coercion that influences the players' choices. Secondly, researchers investigated strategies for exploiting market inefficiencies using quantum-based algorithms, which allow for the utilization of entanglement without compromising security. These approaches demonstrate a capacity to outperform conventional statistical models in identifying patterns within financial data.

This paper examines how prices are set and revenues are maximized in markets with intermediaries, using a specific example of a double auction with intermediaries to buy and sell a single commodity, such as oil. We focus on finding optimal prices and quantities for buyers and sellers through intermediaries, and show that with an infinite number of buyers and sellers, the optimal revenue can be achieved by setting a finite number of price levels. We also investigate how the structure of costs incurred by intermediators affects the market equilibrium, and find that under certain conditions, the optimal revenue occurs when the intermediators' costs are evenly spaced.

Generating summaries that include unfamiliar entities poses difficulties for pre-trained language models, as they cannot automatically extract relevant information from text. To address this challenge, researchers propose an innovative framework that employs entity prompts generated through planning to enhance abstractive summarization. This framework integrates entity recognition and ranking with transformer-based architectures, allowing for the discovery of effective combinations of entities through optimization. In turn, these entity combinations are utilized as input to an abstractive summarization model, as prompts that provide a comprehensive understanding of the source text. Experimental evaluations conducted on the CNN and MSMC datasets demonstrate the proposed framework's ability to outperform existing methods, as it successfully includes unfamiliar entities within generated summaries.

This research demonstrates via Example 1 that if the (n-1)-variable function, g with parameters a1,..., an, exhibits differentiability at point (x1,..., xn), then it can be concluded that the n-variable function, f with parameters a1,..., an, is also differentiable at point x = (x1,..., xn)). Furthermore, this conclusion is not absolute and can only be inferred under the condition that the partial derivatives of f, denoted as f1,..., fn, are continuous. In addition to this finding, several generalizations related to continuous components of the set of differentiable functions on an interval are presented in the concluding remarks.

Previous studies have suggested that people's voices synchronize when they converse, indicating social connection. However, defining and quantifying this synchronization, known as vocal entrainment, is still a challenge. This paper proposes a new method for detecting vocal entrainment in conversations that considers the context and is easy to compute. It compares this approach to existing methods using a database of 24 natural conversations and introduces a database of artificially modified recordings to simulate various social connections.

A recent study on the category of quantum operations has led to the creation of a pre-monoidal category called Lambda-S1, which is based on a specific subset of operations known as unital operations. This category provides an alternative representation of quantum operations within a closed symmetric monoidal framework. By building upon the established category Lambda, which represents quantum states and their associated linear transformations, the introduction of operations as arrows in Lambda-S1 allows for the manipulation of quantum states in a closed and invertible manner. This new structure is distinguished by its unitary nature, where the key property of unital operations is that they map states to states in a consistent and consistent-invertible manner. This property is unique and serves as the defining characteristic of unital operations in Lambda-S1. This definition is found to be equivalent to a more commonly accepted notion of quantum operations, which is based on the principles of trace-preservation and complete positivity. The study demonstrates that Lambda-S1 is a compact closed category, which is characterized by its bidirectional structure and the ability to form adjoint operations through the application of the adjoint functor. This property is made possible by the introduction of a specific operation known as the unital trace, which serves as the context for forming adjoints in Lambda-S1. The study also explores the relationship between Lambda-S1 and its dual category, which is found to be equivalent to the category of unital operations known as S1-Lambda. Analytical calculations have been performed to determine the energy of two quasiparticle excitations above a ground state of Laughlin liquids for any integer and fractional filling factors ν. These quasiparticle excitations include both charge quasiparticle and charge-fluctuation quasiparticle. The energy calculations for the latter are novel in this study. The obtained results match the existing exact numerical data, validating the theoretical framework. Additionally, analytical solutions have established relationships between quasiparticle energies and filling factors through two distinct methods. The derived formulas are expected to contribute to future analytical studies by providing a foundation for understanding quasiparticle energies.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modeling contact processes, S. Gabbert and Ch. Guillet have developed a model that takes into account friction and lubrication. However, this model is a nonlinear variable-order Stokes variational inequality, and its numerical analysis is complex. To address this challenge, researchers have introduced a reduced model that is based on a nonlinear variable-order elliptic equation and is linked to the original Stokes variational inequality through the principle of minimum action. By proving that the reduced model converges to the original model in the L^2 norm, and that it can be efficiently approximated using the finite element method, researchers have shown that the solution can be accurately estimated. Furthermore, numerical experiments have validated the reduced model's effectiveness in glaciology, and have demonstrated its potential applications in modeling contact processes.

Galactic outflows play a crucial role in the evolution of galaxies by limiting star formation through the suppression of gas availability. The relationship between outflows and star formation is complex, with outflows often seen in response to starburst activity yet also regulating starburst intensity. The interplay between these processes is particularly evident in starburst galaxies with prominent outflows. The present study employs observations from the VLA and ALMA to investigate the relationship between outflows and star formation in a starburst galaxy, providing insights into the regulation of starburst activity by outflows. The findings reveal a correlation between outflows and star formation that is spatially dependent, with outflows and star formation exhibiting similar spatial patterns. The data further indicate that outflows are preferentially launched in regions of high star formation, suggesting a causal link between outflows and the suppression of star formation. The results are consistent with a feedback mechanism in which outflows mitigate starburst activity, consistent with the observed decline in starburst intensity over time.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow using the AMPT model for different collision energies. The results showed that the strength of triangular flow has an inverse relationship with collision energy. The ratio of triangular to elliptical flow is directly related to the fourth moment of anisotropic geometry. The characteristics of initial geometry play a crucial role in forming anisotropic flow. The ratio of triangular to elliptical flow in smaller systems is significantly higher than in larger systems and increases as the order of the polynomial used to generate initial geometry decreases.

This document outlines a collaborative framework known as Simultaneous Robotic Framework (SRF), designed to facilitate the development of algorithms for various robotic platforms. Built within the Palletize Your Boat (PYB) framework, a general-purpose simulation environment, SRF enables the efficient creation of robotic simulations, efficient sampling-based operations, and efficient data visualization. By leveraging SRF, researchers and engineers can easily implement and integrate novel robotic algorithms across different platforms without modification, while also allowing for seamless adaptation to new platforms. Furthermore, SRF features a universal planning interface, making it possible to integrate existing and novel planning methods from disparate sources into a unified planning suite.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to impressive results on various computer vision tasks, with image classification being one of the earliest and most fundamental tasks. Researchers have employed pre-training methods on large datasets like ImageNet to achieve state-of-the-art performance in subsequent vision tasks. However, recent studies indicate that using a network designed for monocular depth estimation instead of a typical categorization network yields superior pre-training outcomes for other tasks. To investigate this phenomenon further, we examine whether using depth estimation for pre-training can outperform task-specific supervision and typical categorization pre-training methods. Our analysis reveals that depth estimation pre-training leads to better performance on semantic segmentation, while also providing valuable insights into the potential benefits of depth estimation for pre-training.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane, and also the set of all non-constant harmonic functions defined within the unit ball in the complex plane. We will use these sets to define two categories of mappings from the unit disk to the unit ball in the complex plane and study the optimal radius of convexity for functions that fall within these categories, where this radius is influenced by a specific parameter. By investigating the growth of functions within these categories, we will derive an expression that represents the optimal radius of convexity for functions that fall within these categories.

Inference for Kendall's tau, a non-parametric measure of correlation, can be computationally demanding due to its nature in correlation analysis applications. A new method has been developed to estimate tau by transforming associated binary alternatives of hypotheses testing, where the null hypothesis represents uniformity and the alternative represents non-uniformity. This method, demonstrated with a Brownian motion example, shows that tau estimations follow a standard normal distribution, where the test statistic is the number of paired observations with differing rankings. A corresponding test statistic allows for the creation of a confidence intervals for tau, where the limits are defined as the minimum and maximum possible values that a statistic can take when assuming normal distribution, given the observed value. A simulation study has been conducted to assess the accuracy of this method, where results show that the proposed intervals perform better in terms of coverage and width compared to alternative approaches.

The proliferation of intelligent devices has led to vast amounts of data being generated, which are being leveraged to train high-performing machine learning models. Edge intelligence has emerged as a key innovation in this context, enabling real-time processing of data near the source and facilitating more efficient machine learning applications. Furthermore, edge intelligence can be integrated into automotive networks to improve safety and functionality while safeguarding the privacy of users. This research proposes a framework for maintaining privacy in edge intelligence automotive networks. This framework consists of two primary components: a data encryption mechanism that utilizes advanced techniques like token-based encryption and token aggregation to protect user data, and a privacy-preserving framework for machine learning tasks. This framework employs token aggregation techniques such as Vector of Aggregates on Secret Values and Secure Sum to create composite data elements that can be utilized for machine learning operations, while maintaining the confidentiality of the original user data. This research demonstrates that our framework provides effective protection against inference and attribute disclosure risks.

We investigate a type of homogeneous polynomial that can be related to the Euler characteristic of a compact filtered space. This polynomial, known as the Euler characteristic polynomial, is called "eulerian." Homogeneous polynomials with specific properties are classified as eulers or negative eulers, depending on certain criteria. By utilizing eulers, we demonstrate that for any filtration on a compact orientable manifold, there exists a point where the Euler characteristic changes sign. This point is referred to as an Euler Critical Point (ECP). We also provide a geometric representation of particular manifolds, known as Euler Critical Manifolds (ECM), which are defined by specific conditions on their points. These conditions can be translated into topological constraints, allowing us to identify specific criteria that define ECM. These criteria can also be used to determine the existence of ECPs in specific types of manifolds, even without the condition of orientability.

Our analysis delves into the stability properties of Holling-Tanner predator-prey models incorporating strong Allee effects in both species, with a particular focus on how these effects influence oscillatory behavior. By examining system trajectories in the first quadrant, we identify unbounded orbits and show that in the vast majority of parameters, the long-term system behavior is characterized by the emergence of stable, oscillatory patterns. This investigation also assesses the impact of Allee effects on predator-prey oscillations and identifies conditions for their persistence or disappearance.

The Facet Rotation Method (FRM) has been shown to be an efficient facial reduction strategy for interior point methods in quadratic and linear programming. Building on the theoretical foundation established in Part I, this paper demonstrates that FRM achieves a linear iteration count in a specific setting, providing a comprehensive proof of its efficiency. This iteration count is independent of the initial parameters, including the dimension of the problem. Furthermore, FRM's performance is evaluated under perturbed Newton iterations, revealing that it maintains its efficiency even under such conditions.

In 1990, Leslie J. Bak introduced the NK_1 invariant for graded rings.  For a particular type of graded ring with specific characteristics, we establish that NK_1 vanishes.  This finding has significant implications in the study of graded rings with strong p-adjunction properties.  In the process, we identify an important criterion that must be satisfied in order for certain graded ring conditions to hold uniformly across all degrees.  This criterion is shown to be relevant in the context of graded Einstein rings.

The study investigates how off-shell top quark contributions affect the top quark mass (m_t) determination when using events with a top quark pair and one jet, which is relevant for precise quantum chromodynamics calculations at the Large Hadron Collider. Research focuses on two methods used for m_t calculation: an event-by-event approach and a partial renormalization group equation method. Results show that neglecting the off-shell contribution leads to underestimating m_t by 4-5 MeV for the event-by-event method and 8-10 MeV for the partial RG method. Furthermore, the study provides guidance on applying the event-by-event method to experimental data.

Recent advancements in self-attention-based architectures, specifically Vision Transformers (ViTs), have led to outstanding performance in various computer vision tasks. This paper investigates the efficacy of ViTs in zero-shot face anti-spoofing, a task requiring handling diverse and uneven data. We demonstrate that a compactly structured ViT model, the Cross-ViewTransformer (CV-Net), achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CASIA FVSE2 dataset, outperforming other models, including convolutional neural networks.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising AI paradigm that enables systems to learn optimal policies for complex tasks through interaction with the environment. In the field of autonomous driving, this approach holds significant promise due to its ability to handle the intricacies of real-world tasks. Despite current systems being capable in simulation environments, they still require substantial improvements to apply their knowledge in practical scenarios. Our research involves an in-depth analysis of the current state of deep reinforcement learning in autonomous driving, focusing on the key challenges and potential solutions for deploying these systems in real-world settings effectively.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in tackling complex multi-objective optimization problems, with parallel processing enhancements often employed to accelerate the process, albeit at the cost of evaluation time bias when utilizing a parallel evolutionary algorithm framework. This issue arises due to the uneven selection pressure caused by the asynchronous nature of parallel algorithms, where solutions are more frequently re-evaluated at later stages. This paper introduces a Parent Selection mechanism designed to mitigate evaluation time bias through a novel selection strategy that prioritizes solutions based on their age distribution. Experimental results using a diverse set of high-dimensional multi-objective optimization problems showcase the proposed approach's effectiveness in reducing the impact of evaluation time bias, ultimately resulting in improved diversity and quality on non-dominated frontiers.

The microlensing planet, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, is confirmed to be a cold super-Earth with a mass similar to that of Uranus, orbiting a M-dwarf host with a mass not exceeding 0.50 Msun and a mass ratio of 0.23, making it one of the most massive sub-stellar hosts with such a mass ratio. The object's mass and the host's mass were determined through the analysis of the 2017 microlensing event using the 8-meter Keck telescope's adaptive optics and the Keck Observatory's Extremely Large Telescope's data, along with the data from the Hubble Space Telescope. The analysis revealed a 4.5-sigma detection of the object, indicating a mass of approximately 0.30 Msun, and a 2.5-sigma detection of the host's mass, indicating a mass of approximately 0.20 Msun. The analysis also revealed a 2.5-sigma detection of the object's distance, indicating a distance of approximately 2.8 kiloparsecs, and a 2.5-sigma detection of the object's mass ratio, indicating a mass ratio of approximately 0.23. We investigate the dynamics of open quantum systems under time-varying, non-unitary transformations (Lindblad operators). The evolution is governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and a time-dependent generator of non-unitary evolution (Lindblad operator). By expanding the expanding parametrically regime, we find that for small changes in parameters, the behavior of open quantum systems under time-varying non-unitary transformations closely resembles that of their closed counterparts. The expansion in the weak coupling regime yields expressions for the system's quasienergy distribution that accurately describe its behavior when the system's coupling to its environment is small. The obtained expressions for quasienergy distributions and corresponding decay rates closely match the predictions of existing theories in the high-frequency regime.

Our research focuses on the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ on their long-range magnetic order, examining how the system transitions from ferromagnetism in CePd to spin glass behavior in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with high Rh levels. We used both total neutron cross section measurements and Longitudinal Field Neutron Spectroscopy to investigate the samples' response to external magnetic fields. We discovered significant depolarization in the samples with intermediate Rh levels, but not in those with very high or low levels of Rh, indicating a link between the depolarization and the onset of short-range magnetic correlations. We used the Jaccard index to quantify spin fluctuations in the samples. We observed a correlation between these fluctuations and the samples' electronic hybridization strength, supporting our findings with specific heat measurements. We found that the samples with intermediate Rh levels exhibit two distinct energy scales, indicating a transition from ferromagnetism to spin glass behavior in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$.

A unique phenomenon of HI emissions is frequently observed in regions where high-mass stars are forming. These emissions are often attributed to the ionization of hydrogen gas by the strong ultraviolet radiation emitted by the hottest stars. However, a recent study has found that a particular type of HI emissions, characterized by their narrow line widths, cannot be explained by the radiation emitted by the hottest stars. An alternative explanation suggests that these emissions are instead caused by the radiation emitted by the formation of high-mass stars themselves. A recent study has found that these types of HI emissions are present in a region known as G176.51+00.20, where a high-mass star is actively forming. Data collected from a radio telescope revealed that these emissions are concentrated in areas where the star is actively forming. Analysis of the data also found that these emissions are characterized by their low velocities, indicating that they are physically connected to the region where the high-mass star is forming. An analysis of the data also found that these emissions are consistent with the idea that they are caused by the radiation emitted by the formation of high-mass stars.

We introduce a new class of mixing, piecewise monotonic transformations, known as intermediate beta shifts, which fall between beta shifts and beta expansions, and are characterized by distinct transition intervals between periodic orbit branches, leading to a unique pattern where the sum of leading coefficients of the transfer operator's eigenfunctions exhibits an alternating pattern. By examining the transfer operator of these intermediate beta shifts, we demonstrate the existence of a unique eigenvalue at 1, and show that their spectral measure has a point of differentiability, while also showing that these transformations share certain similarities with beta shifts modified to include a gap, and can be viewed as a form of greedy beta shift, revealing a new approach to understanding the already existing concept.

The CP-averaged observables \Delta\Gamma_s and \Delta'\Delta\Gamma_s, which account for time-dependent decay rate asymmetries, have been measured for the processes Bs->J/\psi\pi+\rho- using LHCb's 2011-2015 data set. Within the context of the factorisation model, the CP-violating phase \phi_s for the pi and rho modes has been determined to be -0.24+/-0.24+(

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks, but their capabilities are limited when dealing with significant changes in data distribution, such as in cross-dataset scenarios. Domain shift occurs when there is a discrepancy between the training and testing data distributions, causing a model with optimal performance on the training data to perform poorly on unseen testing data. This issue can be mitigated by applying domain adaptation techniques to update the model without requiring additional unlabeled data. A new method, called Deep Neural Network Domain Adaptation, aims to address domain shift by incorporating various techniques into a unified framework. Experimental evaluations using ImageNet, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and Stanford Dogs datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework, which has achieved an average improvement of 43.33% in top-1 accuracy compared to models without adaptation.

Consider the set $\mathbb F_q^2$ representing two-dimensional space over a finite field with q elements, where q is a positive power of two. Let C be a curve within the set, defined by a quadratic equation with coefficients from the field, including the special case of a quadric when the coefficient of the linear term vanishes. The main objective of this study is to demonstrate a lower bound on the count of curves in the set, all of the same degree and genus, that cannot be transformed into one another through the process of change of coordinate. Additionally, for the specific scenario of a curve being a quadric, the study provides an approximate measure of the count, close to the order of the curve count, with the difference being at least $\Omega(q^{2-\epsilon})$ for a sufficiently small value of $\epsilon >0$.

A proof without visual aids, using integer arithmetic instead, confirms the existence of at least one equilateral triangle in a tetrahedral grid, by verifying the triangle inequality for all possible distances between pairs of points in the grid.

Graph Neural Networks have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their robust performance in tasks involving graph-structured data. Research has established that graph convolution can be mathematically represented as a deconvolution process, where the goal is to recover the original input feature vector from a given target feature vector, using an adjoint matrix derived from the graph's Laplacian. This study presents a novel, parameterized interpretation of graph convolution, revealing that it can be represented as a deconvolution process involving a specific target feature vector. The research also explores the relationship between graph convolution and Gauß-Weierstrass kernels, providing insights into the operation of graph neural networks, especially in contexts involving group transformations.

The galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420, situated at a distance of 2.05 petameters, is a massive system hosting numerous galaxies. This paper delves into the physical properties of the cluster's galaxies based on spectroscopic data, analyzing 34 member galaxies to determine their redshifts, radial velocities, temperatures, and other characteristics. The results reveal a diverse range of galaxy types, from ellipticals to irregulars, with a notable disparity in temperature readings among the cluster's member galaxies. Furthermore, the study explores the cluster's spatial layout and the movement patterns of its constituent galaxies.

The efficiency of training artificial neural networks can be significantly enhanced by leveraging parallel processing capabilities on graphics processing units (GPUs). Nevertheless, tapping into GPU potential often requires modifying the network's design or employing specialized training algorithms. The Legendre Memory Block network, a class of recurrent neural networks capable of modeling complex functions with fewer parameters, presents an attractive candidate for GPU optimization. This study investigates the effectiveness of parallelization strategies for LMB networks on GPUs, identifying a straightforward approach that effectively harnesses GPU power and validating its performance with real-world time series prediction tasks.

Theoretical models require the presence of feebly interacting particles, which, due to extremely low interaction cross-sections, were previously inaccessible to high-energy physics experiments. Recent advances in theories and detection methods, fueled by a decrease in experimental constraints, now make it possible to detect these particles. This could be achieved through a combination of traditional high-energy experiments and novel approaches such as fixed-target experiments, which have already begun receiving significant attention. For instance, the LHCb RESONANTIA project and the CONCERTO initiative at Fermilab are two prominent examples. As a result, the field of feeble particle research is poised to become an exciting area of active experimental investigation, which will be discussed in this review.

Language development among a group of homogeneous agents is investigated through the naming game, with each agent initially using random names, and then interacting with a dynamic environment by selecting and following an existing name among their peers, chosen purely by chance. As these interactions occur over time, we observe that the number of unique names eventually converges to a stable state, and interestingly, this outcome is unaffected by the presence of external noise, and remarkably, this convergence is accelerated when the agents are highly mobile.

Training neural networks using the mean squared error (MSE) often results in a bias towards fitting the training data's complex patterns rather than the loss function's target. This phenomenon, referred to as spectral bias, can be mitigated by utilizing momentum stochastic gradient descent during neural network training. 

We investigated the effect of momentum on spectral bias in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by both theoretically and experimentally analyzing the relationship between momentum, network depth, and spectral bias. 

Our theoretical analysis revealed that using momentum in combination with the ReLU activation function reduces spectral bias. This reduction in spectral bias was confirmed through our experimental results, where PINNs trained with momentum performed better than those without momentum, especially in large networks. 

These findings suggest that incorporating momentum into the training of deep PINNs can effectively minimize spectral bias and lead to improved performance.

We examine a two-wave system coupled together and introduce damping in one of the waves mimicking muscle tissue behavior from biological models. The waves are represented by a specific type of partial differential equation known as the Helmholtz decomposition. To analyze the system's behavior, we use the Lyapunov function method to measure the rate of energy decay. By proving the system's energy decreases over time and its related norms are stable, we demonstrate that the system's behavior becomes stable even when the damping is replaced with a modified version that only affects certain areas.

Recent advances in reinforcement learning have achieved impressive results in various applications, yet many of these solutions are hindered by being difficult to understand in practical contexts. In domains requiring human expertise, such as robotics, understanding the learned models and rules is essential for building confidence in the system's decision-making processes. This research presents a novel, two-layered approach to reinforcement learning, incorporating model-driven learning through Inductive Logic Programming. This approach enables the learning system to identify underlying rules governing state and action attributes, resulting in increased transparency and enabling the extrapolation of learned knowledge to unseen scenarios. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in a simulated robotic navigation environment.

We've demonstrated that quantum squeezing can induce optical asymmetry by governing the phase shifts experienced by probes in an optical system, with the amount of squeezing determining the direction and degree of asymmetry. Building upon the Jaynes-Cummings model, which features a two-level atom and a single-mode cavity field, our analysis reveals how quantum squeezing affects the unique spectral properties of radiation field. Specifically, we've shown how non-classical field characteristics emerge from the interaction between the atom and the cavity field, with the direction of the non-classical spectrum depending on the sign of the Kerr nonlinearity resulting from the applied squeezing.

This paper investigates a type of minimax problem inspired by Fenton's work, 
where we aim to solve the functional minimization problem:
  min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} max_{\lambda \in \Lambda} J(f,\lambda),
  subject to a set of constraints on f.
  The objective function J(f,\lambda) is defined as the sum of translates of f,
  evaluated at specific points depending on \lambda.
  Our study focuses on several key questions, including:
    (a) Does a solution minimizing max_{\lambda \in \Lambda} J(f,\lambda) exist?
    (b) Is this solution unique?
    (c) Does this solution provide the best possible minimax performance?
  We provide a comprehensive analysis for a broad class of functions \mathcal{F},
  including Holder continuous and Lipschitz continuous functions.
  Our study also examines the relationship between this minimax problem and traditional Chebyshev approximation.
  Finally, we provide a practical application of our results in the field of conformal mapping.

We have proposed an innovative method to use $^{6}$Li isotopes to study interactions between shadow matter and spins. By analyzing the direct and indirect proton capture reactions on $^{6}$Li, and considering various initial targets, it is possible to determine if shadow matter interacts with lithium's proton, neutron, or a combination of both. This interaction could be detected through a significant change in energy spectrum or a direct peak caused by the formation of a compound state with the initial target and shadow matter. Our study provides technical details for the experiment, including recommendations for the energy range and thickness of lithium target needed to identify such interactions.

A common issue in blind image restoration, encompassing blind deblurring, blind denoising, and blind super-resolution, is the lack of clear information about the underlying degradation process. This deficiency severely restricts contemporary deep learning models, which often rely on a predetermined degradation kernel. To overcome this limitation, a novel kernel representation approach is proposed, which models a kernel as a combination of multiple kernel functions. This model can accurately capture various complex degradation processes and has the potential to be adapted to different scenarios. From a theoretical perspective, it is proven that any kernel can be approximated by this kernel representation model, and the approximation accuracy can be optimized through an adaptive algorithm. Furthermore, the model can be easily integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, and experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness in blind image restoration applications.

A semi-direct derivative of the bialgebra Yang-Baxter equation is introduced and termed the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation. The co-algebra structures defined by this equation are linked to the associative rule of matrix multiplication. The equation's solution set can be described using the nonuniform 3-cocycle vector space. The study of these co-algebras is analogous to the rotation of vector spaces by an arbitrary angle. The existence of a special co-algebra structure is demonstrated when the 3-cocycle vector space is finite and has an order that is a power of two. The co-algebra's coalgebra map is shown to be a power series of the 3-cocycle basis elements. The process of forming a semi-direct co-algebra is also a result of rotating the base vector space. The study concludes by defining a co-algebra framework for non-uniform associative bialgebras based on the semi-direct co-algebra structure.

Formal verification through Hoare logic has long been a widely used technique for ensuring the correctness of software based on mathematical logic.  Despite its effectiveness, this method has been limited in its application to programs that can be represented as mathematical abstractions, and has struggled to incorporate more complex, semantically rich specifications of programs that incorporate temporal and other aspects of reality.  This difficulty has led to a significant disparity between the formal verification methods used and the informal methods employed by linguists to describe the progression of time.  This paper presents a framework for formally verifying programs based on a natural language syntax and semantics that incorporates aspects of modal logic, semantic typing, and other formal languages.  This framework is designed to capture the essential features of a programming language, and is used to specify the desired behavior of a program, and to prove that it meets this specification.  This framework is applied to a series of increasingly complex examples, including a simple stack machine, demonstrating its ability to formally verify programs based on natural language descriptions of their behavior.

Distributed consensus is a fundamental concept used in various distributed systems, with many consensus algorithms existing to address different system requirements. However, current state-of-the-art algorithms often prioritize high efficiency over resilience. To address this, we've developed RCanopus, a novel consensus algorithm built on top of the Canopus protocol. Canopus achieves exceptional performance by leveraging a unique 'fast path' for non-failing nodes, while incorporating a robust'safe path' for nodes that may fail to agree. To enhance fault tolerance, RCanopus introduces a new 'check-and-path' mechanism, allowing nodes to quickly determine the likely agreed value and switch to the corresponding 'fast or safe path' without delay. Our evaluation demonstrates RCanopus's ability to achieve high performance and resilience in the face of various failure scenarios, surpassing existing algorithms like PBFT and Raft-Lock.

Recent studies have employed the atomic force microscope's force spectroscopy method to measure the elastic properties of lipid bilayers. Our work builds upon this technique by developing a theoretical framework to analyze data from simulated molecular dynamics simulations. This model considers the effects of thickness variations within the bilayer, resulting in a force relationship characterized by a parabolic coefficient. Our results show that simulations accurately reproduce experimental findings, revealing an optimal level of cholesterol that enhances the elastic modulus. Our theoretical model is further validated by its ability to predict the elastic modulus under different lipid arrangements.

The paper proposes a theoretical model for the formation and collapse of stars and other celestial objects based on Loop Quantum Cosmology principles. It suggests that the critical point in the cosmological evolution occurs when the Ricci scalar curvature reaches its maximum density, triggering a quantum loop transition similar to Planck's. Subsequently, the developed model is applied to the Hamiltonian of the Arnowitt-Deser-Minkowski formalism, describing the stellar core as a quantum state that undergoes a loop transition. The study provides analytical estimates of the stellar core radius, confirming the current understanding of stellar formation and supporting the loop cosmology framework.

A comprehensive dataset of the brightest cosmic rays observed during the first operational phase of the Pierre Auger Observatory has been compiled. This dataset comprises 49 years' worth of data, including 67 events with exceptionally high energy levels exceeding 60 EeV. The catalog also encompasses 19 events exceeding 80 EeV and 4 events surpassing 100 EeV, including the most energetic recorded particle with an energy of 73.2 EeV. The catalog provides detailed information on each event's location, depth, and energy profiles, allowing for a more in-depth examination of the most energetic cosmic particles detected on Earth.

Deep neural network-based object detectors have become the preferred choice for object detection tasks due to their superior performance. However, the uncertainty associated with detection results remains poorly addressed. This study introduces an innovative approach, BayesOD, designed to enhance R-CNN family models for uncertainty estimation in object detection. The framework integrates a model learned with uncertainty and its probability distribution into the object classification branch of the target model, leveraging the probability distribution to introduce uncertainty into the object classification process. The integration method developed for BayesOD is capable of adapting to various deep neural network models. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of BayesOD using various models and datasets, achieving accurate uncertainty estimation and enhanced calibration. The proposed method achieves calibration metrics close to ideal values, outperforming existing calibration methods.

Predicting traffic flow is crucial for city planning and traffic management. Current methods primarily rely on aggregated traffic data, leading to limited understanding of individual traffic episodes. In our research, we introduce a new approach that focuses on specific snatches of traffic movement, allowing us to analyze the predictability of individual episodes. By aggregating diverse datasets including road maps, traffic patterns, and weather information, we create comprehensive traffic models that outperform existing benchmarks, according to our results based on real-world traffic data.

In the context of colored preorders and bifunctors with ordered values, we establish a notion of Gray category, effectively extending and combining categories with twisted values and biproducts of preorders. We show that a Gray category can be structured as a lax extension of a ordinary category defined within a specific monoidal category, where relationships are maintained through the application of the two-dimensional distributive law principle. We further develop a concept of coherence for Gray categories, where categories with minimal coherence are termed strict. Additionally, we define a Gray category as monoidal strict by combining a monoidal category with a strict Gray category defined within it. We demonstrate that a Gray category with a specific symmetry property can be transformed into a category with a different symmetry property through a process involving a modified version of the category, where the new category is created by applying a specific functor to an existing category, where the original category's properties are mapped to a category with a different structure, where the mapping is achieved through the application of a specific natural transformation.

Accurate hippocampal segmentation is crucial for diagnosing and treating various neurological disorders, including epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. In this research, we evaluate the effectiveness of multiple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models for hippocampampal segmentation, and compare our approach with traditional manual annotation methods. The study used the Automatic Hippocampal Annotation competition dataset, and assessed the performance of five CNN models: U-Net, ResNet, Googlenet, VGG16, and SeGNet. The results show that the SeGNet model, combined with an adaptive thresholding technique, yielded the highest Dice coefficient of 0.814 for the hippocampal body, and 0.755 for the head and tail combined, in terms of 95% confidence interval.

In a recent study, researchers demonstrated quantum entanglement by using specific types of light and measuring its properties under specific conditions, which led to an unexpected outcome when certain parameters were increased. The concept of "pigeonhole" in this context refers to an experiment where certain conditions must be met, which leads to an unexpected outcome when certain limits are exceeded. The authors attribute this phenomenon to an overlap of light properties under specific conditions, which leads to an unexpected outcome when certain limits are exceeded. However, in this response, we argue that the expected outcome is expected due to an overlap of light properties under specific conditions, which is consistent with our current understanding of physics. The expected outcome is expected to provide more information about the initial conditions, which can be described using certain mathematical concepts. The authors' initial interpretation of the experiment is incorrect and contradicts our current understanding of physics.

A Monte Carlo simulation was used to model the interaction of galactic cosmic ray particles with Earth's magnetic field and radiative transfer, and then tracked the resulting trapped particles at low Earth orbit heights. Our results indicate that the trapped particle population at this altitude is primarily composed of secondary particles produced through the interaction of primary particles and the magnetic field, and that the trapped particle flux is dominated by particles in the 10-100 MeV energy range.

A comprehensive neural network architecture for graph classification tasks has been proposed, consisting of a skeleton framework that incorporates a Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton, and a local reorganization component to enhance model performance. The framework's design is motivated by the observation that neural networks for graph classification tasks often struggle with scalability and topological biases. To address these challenges, a multi-level framework is developed to capture both local and global features, as well as a dynamic reorganization mechanism to improve model performance. The local reorganization component is based on a node-wise random walk algorithm, which aims to increase the connectivity between nodes in the graph. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a variety of benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods, even when dealing with large-scale graphs.

This paper presents an application of the Huber method in low-rank matrix completion under privacy constraints. The Huber method combines the benefits of robustness and privacy by leveraging the properties of loss functions. We propose a framework based on the Huber method and apply it to private machine learning, specifically in low-rank matrix completion. The framework is evaluated using next-generation sequencing data and a synthetic dataset modelled after the MNIST image dataset. The empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Huber method in private matrix completion.

A new model for interstellar dust has been developed, which combines the effects of small dust particles and larger grains found in the gaps between molecular clouds. By analyzing data on starlight extinction, infrared emission, and polarized light, researchers have found that a specific ratio of these particles is present in the gaps. This ratio remains consistent across different wavelengths, and is primarily composed of larger grains with a characteristic size of approximately 0.1 micrometers. The smaller particles that contribute to polarization are produced locally through interactions and other processes, and their emission is primarily responsible for the overall infrared brightness of the dust. This model has been applied to multiple regions of space and has been used to create maps of dust emission that can be used to study the structure of the Milky Way galaxy.

Observations from ALMA reveal a unique spiral pattern in the circumstellar disk of CIDA 1, surrounding a low-mass star. This spiral shape is thought to result from gravitational interactions between a massive planet and the surrounding dust particles. A model of the disk configuration, based on a planet with a mass similar to that of Jupiter, positioned at a distance of approximately 0.1 astronomical units from the star, effectively explains the appearance of the spiral feature. This model also indicates that the planet's influence on the disk is nearly complete, with surrounding pressure forces overpowering its gravitational pull. As a result, the planet's presence is not expected to hinder its migration, allowing it to continue shaping the surrounding disk configuration. This phenomenon shares similarities with the disk shaping observed in the TW Hydrae system, powered by a massive planet. However, unlike TW Hydrae, CIDA 1 is a system where the planet's presence is directly observable, providing an opportunity to study the effects of planet formation in action.

The Lights Out problem, a well-known single-source tap problem, can be solved efficiently on graphs with specific properties. However, the optimal tap strategy remains unclear even in simple cases, such as regular graphs. A specific tap scenario, known as the Most Taps Problem (MTP), aims to find the minimum number of taps required to solve the Lights Out on a given graph. Research has made significant progress in addressing MTP for certain types of graphs, including bipartite and non-bipartite regular graphs, but the solution for general graphs remains elusive. A notable study proposed a poly-napier algorithm, which yields a 2-О(Δ) approximation factor, but the problem of finding an exact solution within poly(napier) time has yet to be resolved. A different approach, employing the concept of vertex and edge independent sets, has been developed to provide an exact solution for certain types of graphs, such as bipartite and semiregular bipartite graphs, in O(napier log n) time. Furthermore, the algorithm can be adapted to run in O(napier) time for general graphs, resulting in a significant improvement over the previous algorithm's running time.

This paper presents a novel, integrated model of image segmentation and restoration, addressing issues in the field. The proposed model combines a complete segmentation process with a detailed description of the object's boundary, where the boundary description is represented by a non-rigid template. A non-parametric approach is used for the template's description, where vector fields accounting for geometric transformations are used. The model's performance is evaluated using various experiments with real images, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving precise boundary descriptions and accurate segmentation results, where the boundary description is closely linked to the image reconstruction process.

The abstract domain $\mathit{Dom}$ consists of pairs $(x,y)$ where $x$ and $y$ are natural number variables in the program being analyzed. This domain is used for flow-insensitive reachability analysis over a program that increments $x$ and increments and decrements $y$. The program terminates when $y$ reaches $0$. Since reachability interpretations for $(x,y)$ include reachability interpretations for $(x,0)$, these interpretations are inherently forward-predictable. However, standard iterative fixed-point computations using the empty interpretation over the program's $\mathit{Dom}$ fail to terminate. To overcome this issue, a novel technique is proposed that leverages two iterative fixed-point computations: one for program execution phases with rising $y$ values and another for phases with decreasing $y$ values. Both computations are feasible because the program's phase transitions are easily anticipated. The technique is generalizable to programs with multiple phases and applies to other domains where forward-predictability and backward-predictability domains can be identified.

We investigate the topological phonon modes in three-dimensional perovskite oxide structures, where the spin-rotation symmetry and time-reversal symmetry give rise to protected linear bands at the zone center and the Fermi level, respectively. The presence of spin-orbit coupling leads to a unique phase, where the linear bands encircle a core and intersect at the zone center, creating a donut-shaped mode. The donut-shaped mode exhibits exceptional properties, including high robustness and large Berry curvature, and can be manipulated by an external magnetic field due to its sensitivity. The characteristics of the donut-shaped mode suggest that it could serve as a high-performance channel for phonon-based information transfer, enabling fast and stable data processing in magnetic, electric, and gate-biased perovskite systems.

Identifying unusual data points within a dataset is known as outlier detection. These irregular data points stand out from the data set's overall pattern due to their anomaly. Outlier detection is crucial in data analysis as these data points can distort model predictions if not excluded. Several methods have been proposed for detecting outliers in various data contexts, but these often come with a significant drawback: they can only handle specific data types or scales. In this research, we present a novel method for identifying outliers in complex data environments, utilizing a graph-based approach that capitalizes on shortest path distances. Our method converts complex data into a graph structure where the distance between nodes reflects similarity. By examining this graph, we can quickly pinpoint data points that are farthest from the data set's center, effectively identifying outliers in complex data environments. Our approach is unique in that it handles data of any type and scale, making it highly adaptable. Our empirical evaluation using real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in accurately detecting outliers.

We investigate the electromagnetic radiation and thermal stimulation resulting from an atom positioned near a stationary, infinitely thick mirror, where the atom is initially at rest in the ground state. Assuming the atom can occupy two energy states and that its initial state is the lower one, we find that radiation occurs when the atom transitions to the higher energy state and then moves towards the mirror. This movement causes the atom to accelerate towards the mirror, resulting in the emission of non-zero, discrete radiation intensity patterns, where the energy and momentum of the emitted photons are dependent on the atom's position, velocity, and acceleration. These patterns are characterized by the atom's classical trajectory and the distribution of its wave function. Furthermore, we find that the electromagnetic field in the vicinity of the atom is non-zero before the atom moves, where the stimulation results from the interaction between the atom and the reflected electromagnetic field.

Current graph learning methods primarily utilize global metrics to ensure fairness, 
which can be impractical when dealing with real-world datasets divided into 
discrete community groups. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of 
localized fairness within specific community sections, maintaining overall fairness 
on a broader scale. To incorporate this idea, we develop a novel fairness metric 
based on a node's neighborhood and supported by theoretical proofs, and propose a 
weighted optimization approach that maximizes model performance while adhering to 
localized fairness constraints. Experimental results on synthetic and actual 
graphical datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed method in achieving fair 
models with enhanced robustness against community structure changes.

This research focuses on kinetic models describing the reversible activity of enzymes and their steady-state conditions. We analyze and compare two numerical methods for solving these kinetic models: a direct method involving the inverse of a tridiagonal matrix and an iterative approximate method. We found that the direct method is only feasible if the matrix dimensions do not exceed around 200-300 due to computational complexity issues with matrix inversion. In contrast, the iterative approximate method becomes increasingly accurate as model size increases beyond this threshold. We also explored the application of the Bubnov-Galerkin method for developing approximate iterative solutions to the kinetic models.

A search was conducted to find supersymmetry in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, using a 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ dataset collected by the CMS experiment at 13 TeV. The search focused on events with one or two jets, accompanied by significant transverse momentum from invisible particles. These particles were identified through their contribution to a large transverse momentum imbalance. These findings were analyzed in the context of simplified supersymmetry models featuring direct production of charginos and neutralinos in the gauge-mediated model of supersymmetry, as well as in the natural narrow width model and split supersymmetry theories. In these models, the mass of the decayed particle was constrained by the softest superpartner particle production cross section and the mass of the decaying particle. These constraints were further refined by considering the presence of a metastable particle. These findings were also compared to data from the CMS experiment at 13 TeV.
